title: Computable approximations and the limit lemma

based_on.title: Computability theory
based_on.pages: Version 2024-02-25; §16.2, printed/PDF pp.69–70, Definition16.12 and Theorem16.13, with the stage quantifier and limit-computable wording repaired

summary: Allow computable guesses to change finitely often, and prove that their limits are exactly the sets decidable using the halting problem.
abstract: An algorithm may revise its answer as it learns more about a computation. Each individual answer can eventually become correct even when no ordinary algorithm can tell that its final revision has occurred. The limit lemma identifies exactly which membership problems can be solved by such converging computable guesses: they are the problems decidable with access to the halting problem. One direction uses the halting oracle to ask whether another revision will ever occur; the other replaces the oracle by its finite discoveries and gradually increases the computation allowance. This gives a concrete meaning to the second ambiguous level of the arithmetical hierarchy. A computable bound on the final revision would decide the limit set, but pointwise convergence supplies no such bound, even when the limit set itself is decidable.
